traces.question: I went through halfway in 1:42 and 10 km in 47:30. What finish should I expect, and how likely am I to hit the wall?

result.caveat: Fitted on Boston splits; has no weather input. On the 2024 holdout its 80% interval at 35 km covered 74% of runners, so late-race intervals run narrow.

traces.answer:
Expect to finish around 213.5 minutes (about 3:33-3:34), based on your 47.5 min at 10 km and 102 min at halfway [T1]. The model describes your pattern as a "Steady fade" [T1].

The 80% range is 207.48 to 226.75 minutes, and the 95% range is 204.1 to 239.48 minutes [T1]. The upper end is much further from the median than the lower end, so the risk is mostly of slowing down, not of speeding up.

Your chance of hitting the wall (35-40 km pace more than 25% slower than your 10-20 km pace) is about 16% (0.1645) [T1]. That is a minority risk, but not a negligible one.

How far to trust this: the model was fitted on Boston splits and has no weather input, so heat or wind would push you slower than it says. On the 2024 holdout, its 80% interval at 35 km covered only 74% of runners, so the ranges are somewhat too narrow [T1]. Treat the ranges as a bit optimistic, especially the upper bound.

What to do:
1. Keep the second half controlled instead of chasing the clock early, since that is what separates a steady fade from a wall.
2. Keep taking fuel and fluids on schedule, and check the weather. If it is warm, expect to land toward the slower end of the range.

FINAL: finish_min=213.54; wall_risk_pct=16.45

traces.question: My goal is 3:20 in cool weather, but the forecast is 76°F with a 64°F dew point. What finish time should I adjust to, and what even pace per kilometer runs that time?

result.caveat: Fitted on Boston results vs. race-day temperature (baseline 55F or cooler). Dew point is accepted but not used: it did not beat dry-bulb temperature in cross-validation. On its 2015-2019 holdout the model did not beat a flat no-weather guess (2.26% vs 2.15% error), so treat the slowdown as a rough guide.

traces.answer:
Adjust your 3:20 (200 min) goal to about 216 minutes (roughly 3:36), per the heat model: expected slowdown 16.13 min, giving an adjusted finish of 216.13 min [T1]. The model's range for the slowdown is 4.53 to 19.33 min [T1], so the adjusted finish could plausibly be anywhere from about 205 to 219 minutes.

Even pace for 216.13 min over 42.195 km is about 307.33 sec/km, roughly 5:07 per km [T2].

How much to trust this: the model was fitted on Boston results against dry-bulb temperature with a 55F baseline, and the dew point you gave (64F) was not used, because it did not improve accuracy in cross-validation [T1]. On its 2015-2019 holdout it did not beat a flat no-weather guess (2.26% vs 2.15% error), so treat the slowdown as a rough guide, not a precise prediction [T1]. Humid conditions may well be harder than the model shows.

Actions: 1) Start near 5:07/km, or a touch slower, instead of your cool-weather goal pace, and only speed up late if you feel fine. 2) Treat the 216-minute figure as a planning target, and be ready to slow further if the day feels harder than the pace suggests.

FINAL: adjusted_finish_min=216.13; pace_sec_per_km=307.33

traces.answer:
Probably not yet. Feeling great at 25 km is normal, and it doesn't mean you have pace in reserve. In the Boston data, pace stays roughly flat through about 20 km, then climbs steeply from about 30 km onward [2]. The median slowdown over 35-40 km is 15%, and 27% of finishers slow by more than 25% in the closing kilometers [2]. The cards also say the near-universal error is going out too fast, and that the realistic, optimal target for almost everyone is an even split, not a heroic negative split [5]. Mid-pack and first-time marathoners should assume the instinct to push early is a trap [5].

What to do:
1. Hold your current pace through 30 km. The cards say to treat 30 km as the true start of your race and to run the first 30 km conservatively enough to keep pace in reserve while others slow [3]. Keep fueling so glycogen doesn't deplete [3].
2. Past 30 km, if you still feel strong, pick up the effort gradually and judge it by how you feel, not just by your watch. Check splits, but race by effort as fatigue builds [1].
